utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Today we are Thursday. My greetings to the witness, the accused, the Defence teams, and the Prosecution. I would also like to greet all the people who are in and around this courtroom and helping us and I would also like to thank the interpreters for their work. Now I hand the floor to Mr. Scott who will continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Your Honours, good morning. To all those in the courtroom, also good morning. And as the President says, good morning and thank you to all of those in and around the courtroom who are helping us do our jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Dr. Zoric. Doctor, let's try to see if we can move forward a bit. I would like to go to the period now in February 1993. It is correct, is it not, sir, that sometime in February 1993, more approximately the 10th to the 28th of February, there was a major new -- some people called it apparently a census or new registration or reregistration of refugees in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the exact dates but at the time in cooperation with the UNHCR, we did register the refugees and make a census.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, touching back on this concept of refugee status and the various rights or protections that flowed from that status, it is correct, is it not, that refugee status is a temporary form of protection. At one point, I believe you said it was for a period of six months, given for a period of six months, that is the status, subject to continuing extensions if the justifying conditions remained the same or continued. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is mostly how we operated but the status could be extended for less than three months also.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And when this reregistration process was conducted in February 1993, all the persons -- everyone who had been granted refugee status up until that point in time had to reregister and if they did not reregister at that time, they no longer had refugee status; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. That is what was made public because there had been misuse of that status and at that time, we decided to have photographs on the refugee ID cards; that is, we wanted to be more sure about the identity of the respective persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it is also correct, is it not, that as a result or in connection with that reregistration process, the validity period, if you will, the time period for which the refugee status was good, if I can call it that, was in effect, that was shortened to a three-month period; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you to turn to, please, Exhibit -- in the Prosecution binder which you should have there in front of you, if you can please turn to the tab that's marked P 10419. Once you find that, sir, and again as always -- well, you should find a Croatian language version there available to you and if I can direct your attention and the courtroom's attention to paragraph -- specifically, paragraph 38 of that report. Do you have that, sir? Doctor, do you have paragraph 38? While you're looking at that, for the record, that is an ECMM report dated the 7th of February, 1993, which is around the time that we were discussing in the last few minutes, that is, mid-February 1993. Paragraph 38, it says and perhaps you can just follow along and tell me -- I'll ask you if this is essentially a correct statement or summary of what happened at that time. It says that: "On 3 February, one of the coordinating centres, ECMM centres, were told about the announcement by the Office for Displaced People and Refugees that all refugees in Croatia will be registered between 10-28 February, after which they will have refugee status for three months. Anyone not registered would be treated as a foreigner. In addition, all unlicensed refugee centres will be closed and more suitable accommodation found for the refugees. The Bosnian government will advise on which areas are safe and which are not and refugees may be repatriated if they come from safe areas." Is that -- that's an accurate synopsis, isn't it, of the action that was taken in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it also correct, sir, that around this same time, around February 1993, refugees had to begin reporting each month, that is every month, in order to continue their refugee status?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every month, we registered everything that had been handed out as aid, their general condition, their -- the condition of their health, et cetera, and that's why once a month, they were obliged to contact the nearest centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Just moving on to some general points in terms of the refugee situation and again, so there's no misunderstanding in the courtroom and perhaps so we don't have to argue about this, I'm not suggesting that and I've never suggested, in fact, Croatia did not in fact take in a substantial number of persons of all ethnic groups that were fleeing from the conditions in Bosnia. There's no question about that. But at the same time, it is fair to say, is it not, that Croatia was not happy, not particularly happy that these people had come. It created a huge burden on the Croatian government; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anybody is happy if such a burden is placed upon him or her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Correct. And you testified, in fact, to that point in the Tuta-Stela case, counsel, at page 10965, line 22, "We were not happy that these people had come and that we had to take care of them." And that's an understandable point, at least up to a certain point we can all agree on that. It's not a good situation for Croatia, not a good situation for the refugees. And you've also agreed that, in fact that's my second point, you agree, do you not, that being a refugee is not a good thing. It's not something nice. It's a difficult situation for anyone to find themselves in?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact you testified on Tuesday that: "Whether everybody there was happy, well, of course not. Nobody was happy because it's a very sad situation being a refugee. And there could have been dissatisfaction." You also found, would it be fair to say, that these people that were coming into Croatia from these various situations, many of them came with great fear, fear from what they were leaving behind and what would happen to their homes and fear for what their future held; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you also testified and can we all agree that everything else being equal, it was easier being a Croat in Croatia than being a Muslim in Croatia and I'll just remind you on Tuesday, you said, at page 27896, line 12, "It's a fact that the ethnic Croats found it easier to integrate into Croatian society." We can both agree that that's -- was correct, can't we?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is logical that they should have -- they should have a less difficult time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can just touch on the topic, and moving to the topic of the movement of persons who had found themselves in Croatia to third countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's something that I don't quite understand in your cross-examination. You are putting answers or quoting the answers of the witness that he said in -- during the examination in chief. If you are cross-examining it's because you agree with him. Why are you cross-examining with him if that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just certain basic propositions I would like to make sure that we do in fact agree on and it's been very clear on that. I'm laying the foundation, the Chamber can assume that I'm laying a foundation for certain additional questions. I don't think there's any mystery about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we can move to the topic of the movement of persons, again who had found themselves in Croatia at this point to third countries. The Judges I think at this point -- everyone in the courtroom has heard about there was a process at one point that involved something that's been called getting a letter of guarantee from some destination that these people would go and that that would be coupled with something called a transit visa. These are people coming out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If they had a letter of guarantee and a transit visa, they would then be able to move on to some third country. Are you familiar with that practice?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us a bit about your understanding of how these letters of guarantee would be obtained, what that process involved?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We mostly received those letters by mail. Some people handed them in in person. They had a different shape in different countries but they were also officially certified either by notary public or by the -- by some public authority, and it said that a person is willing to take up some other persons and to such people, we gave agreement to go where they were invited to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then there was this second document or aspect of this beside the letter of guarantee -- excuse me. There was something that we've heard about, there's been testimony and evidence in this case, there was something that also would go along with that called a transit visa. How would one obtain one of these transit visas to either cross into Croatia or to travel across Croatia or out of Croatia, if you will, on to another destination?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ODPR did not issue transit visas and transit visa is a colloquial term anyway. We issued a letter in which we stated our agreement for a certain person to be admitted to Croatia at an official border crossing by the Croatian police to go in a certain direction. So we only stated that we agreed to these people being admitted. It was a sort of recommendation but not a visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could just ask you to look at a couple of documents on this point fairly quickly to see if you -- just if you can assist us any further. Can I ask you to go to P 04941, P 04941 which is an HVO document dated the 11th of September, 1993. I show it to you, just simply if you look at the request, it -- as a point of reference it says, "Request for the release from prison of persons who are in possession of letters of guarantee and transit visa for the passage through Croatia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not documents that we issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I understand that, sir. I'm not suggesting otherwise. But you see, then, that this is a document that has 44 individuals listed for -- to be released if they were in possession of these two documents, a letter of guarantee and what's again called here a transit visa. And based on that, sir, I just simply ask you: Did you become aware that that was, as you said maybe a moment ago, a colloquialism but that's what people were describing these additional travel documents, people were calling them transit visas?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I heard some answer but it wasn't in the transcript. Maybe I didn't, and if I didn't, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware that people called it a transit visa. But transit visa were not issued based on such documents. A letter of guarantee had to come from a person who would take up these people and not from those people themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I understand that. Again, there were two documents, at least that's what we've all -- people have told us. There was the letter of guarantee that you could -- someone in another country would take you in, some arrangements would be made. That had to be -- had to have that. You also had to have the second document, something that people called a transit visa. And you say that it was something more like a recommendation, at least in terms of your agency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that letter of guarantee didn't have to be from a third country necessarily, it could be from Croatia also.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt and make one small observation for future purposes. Here's a good example where the gentleman is indicating that he has prior knowledge, he's aware and he's being asked questions and obviously I'm not objecting. I mention this because yesterday during my direct, there was some objections. Here's a clear example of how a witness when he has prior knowledge and you lay a foundation can be asked questions about events to which he was not personally involved in because he had left the -- that office. He was not a member of the parliament and now he's being asked questions. I mention this, Judge Trechsel, because yesterday there seems to be some reservation on some members of the Bench as to this gentleman not being, you know, qualified to comment about a period of time after March 1993 when he was no longer with the ODPR. So I'm making this -- this is a classic example and I commend the Prosecutor for using this technique. I wish to be -- to have the same right accorded to me when I do my direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am not so concerned with procedural questions, I like to go to the crux of the problem. The Prosecutor is showing you a document with 44 names. These people are prisoners. They received letters of guarantee and a transit visa. Those people whose names figure on this list, are they, according to you, from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is that their nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This list was obviously made in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that's what the letterhead says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So those people are foreigners, basically, with regards to your country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, a foreigner, whether he comes from Bosnia and Herzegovina or Hungary or the USA, when such a foreigner would come to your country, did he need a visa and a guarantee to stay for a while in your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a visa was never required for crossing from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia. Foreign citizens, Bosnia-Herzegovinian citizens included, could stay in Croatia and move about up to three months in accordance with the Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners. Longer than that if they had some special reason such as medical treatment, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Hypothetically speaking, let's take an example of a Hungarian person, Hungarian national who comes to your country through -- let's say he leaves Budapest by car, he goes through Zagreb and he wants to visit your country. Would such a person at the time need a transit visa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, because the conditions in Hungary, hypothetical as it may be, were not irregular in any fashion. It was not logical to suppose that anyone from Hungary would apply for refugee status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand you correctly, the transit visa was issued because your authorities believed that these people, because there was a war, needed some financial help and in order to remedy to this type of situation, they were given a transit visa whereas other foreigners who did not want to stay in your country did not need such a document and this is why transit visas were issued and letters of guarantees were given, is that because of a financial or economic reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. Another reason, and not less important, is that we wanted to know who is coming to Croatia from Bosnia-Herzegovina, where they had crossed the border, where they had gone because we needed to establish a database for various services that were searching for people and these databases were the most important resource in this activity. If we hadn't had such registers, we wouldn't have been able to trace people as quickly as we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't want to belabour it but I do want to make very brief response to Mr. Karnavas's comments which I appreciate. Just so the Chamber knows, I am also trying to be consistent with my own practice and do not believe what I did -- said this morning so far was inconsistent with that. I did not expect the witness to have detailed information or to be able to talk about these 44 individuals. I did put the document in front of him just to give a concrete example of a documentation using the term transit visa so that would be maybe less abstract but I did not take him any further into the document than that and therefore, I just want to make sure -- I want to explain, at least in my mind, I've been consistent on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to follow up on the President's questions. Since you've said that, well, someone coming from Hungary, for example, would be able to come into the country for a visit without a visa, without something called a transit visa, but then you mentioned specifically, well, we all know that conditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time are quite different than what was happening in Hungary at that time. Therefore, there was a dimension, there was an aspect, there was a difference, there was something different about people coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And is it not correct, sir, that part of the transit -- what people called a transit visa, whether it was a colloquial term or what, but what people called a transit visa, another purpose of that was to indicate these people were transiting through, they were not staying, there was no intention of them staying in Croatia and that they would not be granted and would not obtain refugee status; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never saw those people. In our recommendations, we stated the facts that were found in the letters of guarantee. If they were from Germany, we gave agreement for them to travel on to Germany. The same applied for people who received letters of guarantee from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question Mr. Scott just put to you is quite interesting and very relevant for that matter. Let's take one of the 44 names, let's take a person on this list and let's say that one of these people has a letter of guarantee to go to Switzerland, for instance, but then he just changes his mind at the last minute and he says, Oh, I really like Zagreb, I would like to stay in Zagreb rather than going to Lozane, for instance. Would he have been able to request a refugee status at that point or would you have said, no, you will not get refugee status and did you ever see or experience some of these cases where people decided just to stay in your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many such cases, Your Honour, cases of people who stayed in Croatia after all, many cases. And I will show information to the counsels how many such people such were even after the date mentioned by the Prosecution, I believe it was June 30th, 1992, how many persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina Croatia had admitted as refugees, how many persons transited, how many returned, how many were refused entry to Croatia, at least as far as we know because the ODPR was not -- had no remit with regard to them. I have all that information on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe the gentleman said 1996 as opposed to 1992 but I don't know. He said June 30th -- my colleague here heard 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I thought he was referring to the questions I put to him yesterday about the 13th July, 1992, decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That could be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure, if he can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just clarify. You've heard some uncertainty perhaps in what you said a moment ago. The date you referred to, could you just give us that again, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the dates that you mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 13 July 1992, at least that's the date that I was referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just once again, to follow-up on the President's questions, we all know that human beings are complicated, changeable people -- changeable beings, sure, some people arrived in Croatia, got to Zagreb, decided they wanted to stay and we can all agree that undoubtedly happened. But when your office received the paperwork, when you received -- when you were looking at these letters of guarantee and what some people called a transit visa for the purposes of passing through Croatia on to Germany or some place else, your full understanding -- and when I say "your" not just you personally but ODPR, the Croatian government's understanding and intention was that these people would be passing through Croatia for a short time, transiting on to another location, and they would not be staying in Croatia as refugees; correct? Maybe some did, but that was not the intention or understanding; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to the other side of this situation if we can, that is where the people were coming from and I wanted to pick up on something that you touched on, I believe, yesterday. That you said something to the effect that depending on where people came from, they could be denied refugee status or entry because you might say, well, there's no reason for someone from that location to be considered a refugee. And in fact, in the Tuta-Stela case, you used the example of Siroki Brijeg and presumably a Croat from Siroki Brijeg, you said that remained a free area, what you considered a "free area" throughout the war and you would not have considered or approved any Croat coming from Siroki Brijeg as a refugee. If counsel wants to check me on that that can be found at 11005, line 10. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so everyone in the courtroom understands these scenarios, you would agree about me, wouldn't you, that a particular area might be safe for some people or one ethnic group and not safe for another ethnic group; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct too. And we acknowledged well-based fear as a reason for refugee status and there were many cases in which our decisions of a general character were later reviewed and adapted to the needs of the individual person. So, if the office said that persons came from a certain municipality not affected by the war such as Siroki Brijeg, are not entitled to refugee status, still, there were people from these such areas who had received -- who came as refugees but we cancelled their refugee status. But if they could provide plausible reasons for their being a refugee then we would grant that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I was listening to you and there is another legal problem that is has just cropped up. This Croat from Siroki Brijeg, I suppose is a national of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he is a Croat by ethnicity, nevertheless, he is a national of the Republic of BiH, but in your -- under your law, aren't Croats granted dual citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct and true that Croats, even though they do not reside in the Republic of Croatia may apply for and be granted Croatian citizenship, not only the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina but also those living elsewhere if the legislation of the country they reside in allows for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this Croat person from Siroki Brijeg, an area that is not affected by the conflicts, if they were to apply for Croatian citizenship, could they, being a Croatian national, be regarded as a refugee because I'm under the impression that you can't be a refugee in your own country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't grant refugee status to the people from Siroki Brijeg. The problem may be of a legal nature if the refugees sought Croatian citizenship and were granted it and at that point, they should have been deprived of their refugee status. They could no longer be refugees, rather, they embarked upon a so-called integration process. This was a procedure that we adopted in accordance with the recommendations of the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One very last question because many of the accused said that they had dual citizenship. I understood that their dual citizenship was granted automatically, you did not need to apply for it, as I understood, but you seem to say that a Croat who lives abroad, outside the country, can have the Croatian nationality but he has to apply for it. So can you enlighten me on this? Is this a dual citizen or a citizenship by right or do you have to apply for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to the extent I'm able to explain the matter, all the inhabitants of Croatia who resided in Croatia whose place of permanent residence was in that former republic of that former state automatically became the citizens of the Republic of Croatia, nationals of the Republic of Croatia regardless of their ethnic background. Everyone else had to apply for citizenship including the Croats living outside Croatia. According to the law, they had to prove ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, a Croat who lived in Prozor, who went to school there and then moves to Croatia, does he have to apply for Croatian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. He could have applied for citizenship in one of the consulates, for instance, that Croatia had in Bosnia-Herzegovina and if that person was eligible then he could have been granted citizenship. Otherwise, he could have sought citizenship in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can an additional question be put to that because your question was, "Should that Croat from Prozor have to apply for citizenship upon his arrival in Croatia ..." and this is where a misunderstanding may arise because the witness said that the individual may have, could have applied for citizenship rather than -- it's not a must. So if you could reput the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat, in this case, you have a Croat who lives in Prozor and goes to school there for years and years and then decides to go to Croatia for some reasons, whatever they may be. Is he going to be a Croat automatically? Is he then going to be given an ID card, a Croatian passport as a Croatian national or does he have to apply for his Croatian national to be acknowledged before he is given an ID card or a passport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, such an individual would be required to apply for citizenship. Citizenship was not granted automatically. I will give you an illustration: Even today there are Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina who have declared themselves to be Croats but have not applied for and consequently have not been granted Croatian citizenship. One of them was at the recent elections elected one of the members of the BH Presidency and he stated explicitly that he was not a Croat national, he never asked for Croatian citizenship, he's a national of Bosnia-Herzegovina, though an ethnic Croat living in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for your answers. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Doctor, now that we've broached this topic, it might be worth while, it might assist everyone, at least some of us in the courtroom on this side of the courtroom and perhaps the Judges to pursue it a bit longer. The impression one has, and you can tell me if I am wrong, is that given the awakening of the national Croatian spirit, the Tudjman government coming into power, the HDZ, there was a desire to promote, if you will, Croatian citizenship, on a global basis that any person considered themselves a Croat in the diaspora living in the United States, Australia, Canada, Germany, if you wanted to get -- if you wanted Croatian citizenship, and of course had you to jump through some hoops which we'll come to in a moment, but there was a policy to encourage or maybe a fairly liberal attitude to gaining Croatian citizenship for people who were Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not describe that position as liberal at all. Individuals had to collect the relevant documentation and submit it to the competent office service of the consulate and meet all the requirements under the law. If these were met, then they became nationals. I believe that some people even voiced their displeasure with the slow pace of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we all understand bureaucracies, I think, in every country. But my question to you is this and if I'm wrong then please set us straight because there may be a number of people in the courtroom who have thought about this. Was there some advantage or different process or different rules for a Croat to obtain citizenship rather than anyone in the world can apply to be naturalized as a citizen. That is, I am not Dutch by ethnicity but if I live here long enough and I want to become a naturalized citizen, I can apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I'm going to object to the scope of the question on the grounds of relevancy. I don't see why this is relevant, number one, and I think it is also beyond the scope of direct examination. I may wish to be a Swiss citizen, it doesn't mean that Switzerland is going to embrace me simply because I come from a particular country, you know. Or I may wish to be Greek, I have to go through the procedures but I don't see what this has to do with the direct examination especially given the narrow scope of the gentleman's testimony. Now, there will be, I can assure Mr. Scott and everyone else, there will be a witness that will be coming very shortly who was from the diaspora who participated in the events and ultimately became an ambassador for Croatia and perhaps he might be the one that might be more relevant to ask these sorts of questions. But this gentleman here, given the scope of the direct examination, I fail to see how this line of questioning is relevant and if it is relevant, I would like to know how. And I would like a ruling from the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me respond first, Your Honour, please, before the Chamber deliberates. First, number one, I'm following up on the President's questions. Mr. President, you raised this area and I think it is relevant, having said that. I think it is relevant to the case because we're dealing with the whole scope of the status and rights of people travelling in and their rights once arriving in Croatia. And you had Muslims going there, you also had Croats going there and I do think that it could be a difference if a person -- if a Bosnian Croat arrives in Zagreb and can easily then obtain Croatian citizenship and stay, because he is a Croat, that may be a fundamentally different situation than what the situation that the Muslim persons arriving in Zagreb found themselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't see how that is part of a joint criminal enterprise or a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No one's saying it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't see what the relevance then is. What is the relevancy and if I may and I don't wish to take any time from the Prosecution, the question from the Judge, from the Bench and from Mr. Scott was basically somebody coming in and it's very clear, they can come in and stay up to three months and after that, they either have to get permission or they have to seek refugee status if that's the case. That's the base -- now if he wants to limit the scope of his question, fine. I don't wish in any way to interfere with his cross-examination but I don't see how this is advancing either side in getting -- in helping the Court get to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Karnavas, you are the one who called this witness to talk about the refugee status of displaced persons. That's a very important legal aspect. Based on that, it is interesting to know what was their procedure to obtain this status of a refugee, to know who would stay and who would go, whether there were cases of discrimination. So basically this is what the Prosecution tries to ascertain with this witness. So these are topics that are relevant. We're not wasting our time, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we're very clear because I don't want the Bench assuming -- any one of the members of the Bench assuming that I'm somehow trying to keep you from knowing the facts. I have no objection to that. But as far as who can be granted citizenship and to say had that somehow if someone who is of a Muslim ethnicity or a Slovenian or a Hungarian or whoever who is coming from the former Yugoslavia cannot get citizenship, somehow has relevance to the case. I don't see that. If we stick to issues of refugee status, status as far as staying in the country, benefits, that sort of stuff, I totally -- I have no problem with that. Beyond that, I think we need to have a narrower scope. That's all I'm saying and I just made my objection and I'll sit down for the rest of the period on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to fully endorse what my colleague Karnavas stated, that very soon we will have a witness here who was an ambassador of Croatia to Sarajevo during the war and he can explain the matters concerning the granting of citizenship. I'm stating this because the Prosecutor in his latest submission on why he insisted on these questions stated that it was far easier for a Croat who arrived to Croatia as a refugee from Bosnia to be granted citizenship than a Muslim. I believe that this witness does not have the required knowledge unlike the witness, the former ambassador to Sarajevo who is soon to be called. It would be far more helpful to listen to the answers of that witness as to how many Muslims were granted Croatian citizenship and we're talking about very high figures during the war and that is something I believe this witness is not familiar with, either with the procedures or with the cases of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina being granted Croatian citizenship. For that reason, I believe that these matters should be raised at the point when the witness with requisite knowledge takes the stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In other words, Ms. Nozica, you do not say that this is an irrelevant question, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour, for giving me the opportunity to state that. I do believe that it is very relevant; I am only afraid that we are taking one direction only concerning only Croats having been granted citizenship. I believe that at the same time, we have to also discuss the matter of the Muslims having been granted citizenship and only then shall we have the complete picture of how it worked during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. There was no suggestion that there were not situations where Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina were granted Croatian citizenship. I have not stated that position. We are trying to get a better understanding. This is a witness who has been a senior official, an ambassador himself, a member of parliament, a person extensively involved in the coming of people into his country and he may be able to assist us, he may not. I think if I could just ask a few more questions, as they say in the movies, if the Chamber would grant me a bit of latitude, I think we can connect up the relevance to this if the witness can help us. If he can't help us, then we'll go on in a couple of moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We think that this is relevant and we took due note of the fact that there were Muslims who could also become Croatian citizens but, of course, it is a possibility, maybe it was also a reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, let me go back to -- what I was trying to illustrate simply is we all know -- well, I think we know, I think most people in the courtroom know that most countries provide for a naturalization process that is by which virtually anyone can apply for citizenship in another country, their non-native country. And I simply pick the example of -- I find myself in the Netherlands. I am not Dutch by birth or ethnicity, if there is Dutch ethnicity and I suppose there is, but if I decide I want to stay in the Netherlands and obtain Dutch citizenship, I can apply for that. I can be naturalized and become a Dutch citizen. But that doesn't turn on me being Dutch, it isn't dependant on my Dutchness, if you will. So are you telling the Chamber that based on all of that, that a Croat who -- a Croat in Australia or the United States or in Bosnia-Herzegovina had no other additional rights or better opportunity, if you will, to become a Croat citizen than any other person who would follow the naturalization process? So a Croat in Bosnia-Herzegovina had no better opportunity or more -- a different advantage to obtain Croatian citizenship than a person from -- applying from, let's say, Germany who was not Croat? A German citizen who applies, he's not Croat, he just wants to apply and be a -- wants to become a Croat citizen. So you're saying the Croats from all over the world, the Croats in the diaspora that the HDZ and that Tudjman were reaching out to, they had no more right to become Croatian citizens than anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, now we're going about HDZ and Tudjman. We heard from the first, very first witness, we already have testimony and I will concede the point for the record, I will concede the point for the record, for the first time, Croatia is a nation recognised within international boundaries. Based on their constitution it allowed all Croats no matter where they were, whether they were from Cleveland, Ohio, where I come from, where there is a very large Croatian community, all of them had a right to apply for Croatian citizenship just as when Greece became a member of the European union later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Are you testifying again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, you should not testify, Mr. Karnavas. I think this is simply not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We've had testimony to this and, Your Honour, I am shocked that you have not objected because of the form of the question. The gentleman never suggested that the Croats did not, you know, did not -- had the same footing as others. Look at the previous testimony today. You are very quick to object to me, you are very quick to jump on me and it seems sometimes personal but when it comes to the Prosecution and they are trying to assume facts that are not in evidence, there is no objection. The gentleman never indicated, never indicated and we've had testimony, Your Honour, so it's not me testifying. We've had testimony, we've had the constitution, this came into the Prosecution's case, it came through the very first witness. Croats around the world could get citizenship and of course they had better or more special privileges but the testimony has been that they still had to make an application. That was my reason why I indicated if I wanted to be a Swiss citizen, if a Croat wanted to become a Slovenian citizen they would have to, in the Slovak, a Slovenian from the United States, who would have the better chance? Who would have the more opportunities? Who would have the better privilege of becoming a Slovenian citizen? It depends on the constitution. How is this relevant to the case? How is this relevant to the joint criminal enterprise. You jump on me, Judge Trechsel, but I want to know why don't you stop the Prosecution? Why don't you suggest that he is asking questions with facts that are not in evidence or that he's twisting the witness's testimony? This is why I think there is a double standard. Yesterday I was prevented from going into areas, on the assumption that this gentleman, beyond a certain point in 1993, could not testify. Now we're asking him questions of which he is not an expert. You've not objected to him not being an expert but all of a sudden we're allowing it. I'm allowing it because the Prosecution has laid a foundation. I'm merely just showing and I'm frustrated today because there is a double standard in this court. Especially when you come to objecting to me, Judge Trechsel and I think sometimes it's personal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hope that it's not the case but it appears this way. It appears and I'm talking about perceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I fail to understand very well what the problem was about, the problem raised by Mr. Scott or yourself. We've had a witness who's held high positions, political administrative positions within this office. He was an ambassador. Therefore, somebody who is able to understand a question and to answer it. Furthermore, in terms of citizenship he is competent because he was an ambassador of his country to Sarajevo. Although there is a consulate, I suppose he had to deal with issues related to citizenship so he knows the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is an established fact in this case that Croats around the world could get citizenship. That's a known fact. And everybody else -- so why are we belabouring the point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't even dealt with that once you're on your feet. You don't even know what I'm going to say and you rise to speak about Croats from the USA who have that citizenship. That's not my topic. I'm interested in knowing what the procedure was to obtain citizenship. Mr. Scott's case, and that was the purpose of his question, was to say that in terms of citizenship in the way it was treated, there was -- there were various reasons to obtain it, that's the question he wanted to put to the witness. It may be that the witness would say no, there was no discrimination, the fact that you were an HDZ member did not give you citizenship. I don't know. I don't even know what the witness is about to answer and you are both belabouring the point on answers that can have legal answers because there were laws and regulations in Croatia, there was a practice in place to obtain citizenship. Let us not forget that in Croatia, and you yourself highlighted this through documents, there were hundreds of thousands of refugees. 1.800.000 refugees at one point in time. So among these people, there must be people who applied for Croatian citizenship and it may be that the witness can tell us that. He can tell us that as far as he knows, there were Muslims who became Croats or not. Rather than spend too much time on those other issues, I think we should deal with these substantial issues. The Prosecutor will put a question, the witness his answer and then you have the possibility in redirect to come back to this subject. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm going to make an issue and I believe that we are to calm down and to talk about these questions with no particular vehemence, but at the same time, I do agree that this issue, in general, is a topic which could and should be discussed and questions be put about it in our Trial Chamber. I would like to say, knowing the Hungarian regulations, that we do have also citizenship for those Hungarians who left the country before 1945, before 1956, after 1956 and -- but they have to apply for it. They get a passport but with no -- in a way, no equal rights with the Hungarian citizens in situ, who are in Hungary, because of course they cannot apply for the same benefits, et cetera, like the Hungarians living in Hungary. Now, the same situation doesn't apply to those Hungarians with Hungarian ethnicity who live around Hungary. As you know we have quite a big number of them starting from Vojvodina and also a few in Croatia but many of them in Transylvania, Romania and in Slovakia. Now, the issue I believe that it could be discussed here if there was any kind of discrimination on that basis and therefore I believe that the topic could be addressed too -- it may be a situation that it could be addressed later on when we have another witness here. I do not exclude this possibility which was mentioned by Mr. Karnavas. At the same time, I think that again, I would like to emphasise that they should remain calm about it and of course Mr. Scott should conduct his cross-examination in view of the fact that it is not the, I would say, the major issue here with this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I certainly never intended that we would get so bogged down in this. I thought that following up to the President's questions there might be a few questions that would assist the Chamber and assist everyone in the courtroom and I had no idea that we would wind up being -- become enmeshed in such a situation. I don't know why it's so troubling to counsel -- I just don't understand why it's such an apparently touchy issue. Mr. Karnavas himself, and I agree with Judge Trechsel as I've said and what counsel says is not testimony and that goes for me too. And simply to make the point and the reason I was asking the questions that I was asking, I was just trying to get some basic answers to, Mr. Karnavas himself answered not in an evidentiary way but just so every in the courtroom knows where we are, on page 25 today starting at line 15, Mr. Karnavas said, "Croats around the world could get citizenship and of course they had better or more special privileges in connection with obtaining citizenship." Now that's my whole point. I've never said Muslims couldn't obtain Croatian citizenship. They probably did. I don't dispute that for a second. What we were trying -- all we are trying to establish was because of that policy, the very policy that Mr. Karnavas said exists, the Croats had a different situation, with more privileges, if the witness could just assist us and say apart from the right of any person anywhere in the world to apply for naturalized citizenship, and again I use the example of if I want to become a Dutch citizen, I can apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But wasn't there, sir, a different procedure by which persons who were Croat or who claimed to be "Croat" could become Croatian citizens? Or they could just apply to become naturalized just like everybody else. It's a very simple question, really. Were there two procedures or was there just one that applied to everybody?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what exactly your last question was. You asked about a German applying for Croatian citizenship or is it something else? Is it about Bosniaks and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me try one more time in the interests of time and I promise the Chamber that if we can't make headway, I'll move on because there are other things that I want to cover with the witness but one last chance. Witness, we all know, I think -- you understand that anyone could apply to become a naturalized -- anyone anywhere could apply to become naturalized Croatian citizen?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: However, we've heard in the case, the Judges have heard, all of us have heard that, you know, people who are Croatian citizens around the world can vote in the HDZ, they can even get elected to parliament because they are Croats and Croats everywhere, you know, have this special relationship. Maybe it's a good thing, the special relationship with their home country, with Croatia, but the point is apart from the naturalization process, did these Croats around other places whether it was Australia or the United States or Bosnia, if you were a Croat, was there some different, special arrangement that applied for obtaining citizenship other than just the normal naturalization process?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a law in Croatia that regulates these issues. This law provides for different categories, different conditions, different possibilities. You could apply for citizenship and be denied it. Alternatively, you could fulfill certain conditions and then be granted the citizenship. An alien who had been living in Croatia for five years without interruption fulfills the basic condition. Then you had to prove that you know the language and customs of the country where you want to live in and another possibility was that citizenship was offered to someone if it was in the interest of the Republic of Croatia such as public personalities and top sports people, et cetera. So Croatian citizenship could be obtained on different grounds, but all these possibilities were regulated by the law and I agree that under this law, anybody could apply for citizenship but I also agree that not everybody had to be granted citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I promised I would move on so I will. I think the Chamber knows the question that is pending and I guess we'll hope to get from a future witness but I promised I would move on so I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you would agree, sir, would you not that in terms of people returning to the -- facing the prospect of returning, the possibility of returning to the place from which they had fled, left under various conditions, they might -- these people might have the right on paper to return, someone might say, "Well, go forth and go back to your home country and be happy," but having that right on paper and actually being able to go back and live in that same situation can be two very different things; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some situations, that is certainly what it could have been like. Safety is certainly the first pre-condition for sustainable return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Safety being as you say, certainly, a first condition. Also the conditions that existed that -- the conditions in that area not just safety but would you agree whether they had anything to return to. Did their house still exist? Would there be jobs there? Would they be able to live there? Was there any community left there or had the community been destroyed? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The other condition is the sustainability of that return or the first or all conditions together as well as that the return had to be voluntary. Unfortunately in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is still many areas without any return and I doubt there will be return to those areas any time soon because the conditions are not favourable. But return was possible at two levels. One type of return is to the very place you had come from and the other type is return to your country. If the conditions did not exist, the conditions you mentioned, if you don't have your house, if you don't feel safe, but at least you could be in your country. I mentioned the example of Croatia. We were called upon by many European countries to receive people from Vukovar to Croatia to take them back again after three or four years or so even though the town was not liberated and their houses had not been renovated, but they returned to their country who continued to take care of them. In the same way, refugees, in some cases refugees from BiH, could return to their country in which case they would no longer be refugees but become displaced persons in BiH and there were many such situations. The first step in the return process is the return to the so-called majority area. The programmes we conducted, I spoke about that yesterday or the day before yesterday, was called "closer to home." You will agree with me, I believe ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just to clarify today, in 2008, are there still refugees in Croatia from Bosnia and Herzegovina, for instance, coming from Mostar who were unable to go back to their city of origin and that still live in Croatia as such? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe there are still such refugees, several thousand, both the ones and the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, you said there are several thousand people living in that situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are not great numbers, but as far as I know, there are still people with that status in Croatia. The office is still in existence, it has a different name though, it's an agency in a Croatian line ministry but there are still people in Croatia with that status be it for the reason that reconstruction is not yet completed or because return is not yet possible. The numbers are not great but unfortunately, there are still such people around even so many years after the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, perhaps just to move us forward as quickly as possible on this point let me refer you back to your previous testimony and just ask you if you agree that that's an accurate assessment. You were talking about refugees and displaced persons at that time, that being people being returned and you said -- counsel, I am looking at page 11022, line 24, starting at line 24. You testified, sir, "Where could they go? To devastated areas? To mined areas," that is areas where there are mines, "without reconstruction so it took another two or three years during which it was impossible to return. And besides, during -- if you live as one of these type of person, refugee or displaced person, for six or seven years, so many things change in your life, children grow up, get used to living in one place. They've already left some place else. It's very difficult for them to go back." Now, would you stand by that same statement today?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I believe that's a very real image you've painted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic please, if we could, and that is not the ODPR that you worked in in Croatia but an agency by essentially the same name or in fact indeed the same name, the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees that was established in Herceg-Bosna, and can you tell the Judges whether in your capacities as an official of the Croatian ODPR, did you interact and deal with counterparts, if you will, people at the ODPR Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did sometimes, either with that office or with the office of the Sarajevo government or with a similar office or agency or body that was active in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And concerning the people at the ODPR Herceg-Bosna, do you recall and can you assist the Judges with the names of any persons that you dealt with in that agency?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was several people who were head of that office successively, one of them was Martin Raguz. I am not sure whether he was the first or the second. And the other's name was Tadic. The gentleman in charge of that office in Sarajevo was called Recica and in Banja Luka, I know that he -- later on when I was in Sarajevo, I was head of the national bank, but what was his name again, Vladusic, Mr. Vladusic. I believe that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the Mr. Tadic who was the person I think you said in addition to Mr. Martin Raguz who was involved in the Herzegovina region, would it be correct that that was Darinko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Darinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were involved, in fact, if you will, recruiting Mr. Tadic, you and I believe another individual, a colleague of yours or a friend named Ciro Grubisic. You and Mr. Grubisic sort of recruited Darinko Tadic to establish the ODPR in Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was in no position to do that. I didn't have the power to do so, nor was it possible for me. No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me see if I can prod your memory a bit more and then we can move on. So you don't recall meeting with Mr. Tadic in Zagreb in about October 1992 for the purposes of discussing the establishment of the ODPR in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that meeting but I know that Mr. Tadic had a humanitarian organisation in Zagreb and later on I saw him but I learned from TV that he had become head of that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, do you recall, in fact after a meeting, if you can recall, just testing your memory a bit further, do you recall after meeting with Mr. Tadic in Zagreb, travelling then, that you actually travelled with Mr. Tadic to Mostar where you met with Jadranko Prlic to establish the ODPR in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not travel with Mr. Tadic, that's for sure, and I may have spoken with Mr. Prlic about the need to establish such an office. As I said earlier, it was my intention and my wish for them to do that work themselves and thus, I confirmed that I wanted to help Mr. Prlic and everybody else so that they be able to organise humanitarian aid themselves and everything else that concerns them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You say, sir, that you may have met Mr. Prlic. You may have met him or are you now telling the Chamber that now that you've had a chance to think about it for a few more moments, you did, in fact, meet -- deal with Mr. Prlic on this topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe he said I may have spoken as to may have met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said you may have spoken to him. Did you, in fact, do you recall now in fact that you did speak with him and if so, on one occasion or on multiple occasions?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have spoken about that already. It is very difficult for me to recall specific dates. It is not a secret that I did speak to him. And I think that's very logical. Many organisations from abroad came to Croatia to assist us and I see nothing strange in my attempts to help the people in BiH, at least by giving advice. It would have been strange to have done otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, I don't see anything strange about it either. I'm just asking just for some information. So when you said that it's no secret that you spoke with Mr. Prlic on this topic, did you speak with him on one occasion or many different occasions?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell now but I think it was once or twice and those were conversations in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you speak with him -- were these conversations on the telephone or did you ever speak with Mr. Prlic face to face, say, in a meeting or something such as that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I spoke to him for at least two and a half hours because that's how long it takes to drive from Zagreb to Grac and in the winter of 1992, we rode to Grac together. I wanted to tell him about how he can collect more humanitarian aid that he needed and certainly we were not quiet during that ride, we spoke, but I really cannot remember precisely what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you assist the Judges with what was the purpose of you and Mr. Prlic travelling in the car for two and a half hours to Grac together? Why were you going to Grac at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted him to meet people from Austrian humanitarian organisations which had sent some aid down there and I wanted him to establish direct contact so that they may be in direct contact from then on and receive aid because until that time, we were often contacted by individuals from BiH and that was a burden -- an additional burden in our regular work. I believe that we should do our work and they should do theirs rather than us working for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me. If you'll let me stop you there because of time. Can you tell us, please, who did you understand Mr. Prlic to be, sitting in this car with him for two and a half hours? How did he introduce himself? Who did you understand Mr. Prlic to be at that time in terms of any position or functions that he held?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he held a high position in Herceg-Bosna, but I don't remember which position exactly. But he was certainly a high-ranking official.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you have any other communications or conversations or meetings with Mr. Prlic following this trip to Grac?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely. I practically didn't see him until I went to Sarajevo. If I saw him, it was not these -- these encounters were not planned, they were just in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say until you saw him in Sarajevo that's when you took up -- I assume you're referencing when you took up your ambassadorial duties in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was ambassador and he was Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it is time to take a break so we'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move on to another topic now, please. Before I do that, just to touch on some of your additional background. We understand already that you were elected to parliament in 1993 and served until sometime in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And while you were a member of parliament, I believe you served in the position -- in addition to being a member, you were the vice-president of the Chamber of Counties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us who perhaps know a bit less about it than some in the courtroom, the Chamber of Counties, that is one of the two chambers of the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, is that considered to be the higher chamber or the lower chamber or maybe that doesn't apply at all but where does it fit into the structure?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the Croatian parliament had two chambers whereas now it has only one chamber following the amendment to the constitution. Which of the two was higher or lower, well, they thought that they were the higher chamber and we thought that we were and the debate never ended, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that, Dr. Zoric. Mr. Stringer and I have that same argument all the time. But at the time in -- when you held this position, I realise there was now only one Chamber, but at the time there were two, you said it was the Chamber of Counties, what was the other chamber called?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, you have the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I think that there is an error in the transcript which changes the meaning of the answer. These are lines 22 to 25 and that's in the following, and that's the witness said that with the amendment to the constitution, it was after the constitution was amended that the Croatian parliament had only one chamber and not that after the change to the constitution there were two chambers and that's when the witness referred to the debate. The debate referred to the situation before the amendment to the constitution because that's the time when there were two chambers. So the debate about which of the chambers was more important was not related to the amendment to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could just proceed to get for purposes of the record what was the name of the other chamber? You were vice-president of the Chamber of Counties. At the time when there were two chambers, what was the name of the other chamber?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the chambers was called the Chamber of Deputies and the other the Chamber of Counties and I was in the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And how did you get to be the vice-president of the Chamber of Counties? Can you tell us very briefly just how does one get selected or appointed vice-president?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vice-president is not appointed, rather, he is elected at the constituent session. There were two vice-presidents and I was one of them. The deputies elect a vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And at the time that you were a member of the Croatian parliament, you were a member of the Social Liberal Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that is sometimes abbreviated the HSLS?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at the time, sir, it's correct, is it not, that the HSLS was the largest opposition party in Croatia, that is, in opposition to the HDZ which was in power at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you've told us that sometime later, you became the Croatian ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just, and I'm not asking anything sinister about this but just so that the record is clear, were you -- was that -- were you considered the Croatian ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina or did you have some position that had ambassadorial functions perhaps associated with it but different than being the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the ambassador. I don't know what other function there could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And you held that position for how long?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one do you mean, the ambassadorial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit under two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: From when to when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: January 1999 through to November 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, based on all these positions that you've held including some actually quite senior positions, vice-president of the chamber of parliament, ambassador, a party leader, would you agree with me, sir, that in various of those functions, you've experienced that life, and sometimes in particular political life can be complicated?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to be active in politics but I wasn't that good at it, which is the reason why I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That might be a good thing. But when you were in political life or in any life, for that matter, one can have at the same time multiple agendas, multiple goals in life in business or personal life. In fact, one can have competing agendas; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean competing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sometimes, I think, would you agree that in life, again, both perhaps personal life and in business or political life, one may have several different agendas or objectives and they may even to some extent conflict with each other but you try to balance them out as best you can; correct? At least I do. I don't know how you live your life but ... or do you just have, at any given point in your life, sir, do you just have one agenda, one objective at a time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never had only one agenda. I tried to engage in politics but I wasn't that successful at it which is why I stopped. I am good -- I'm a good businessman and I decided to engage in my profession and I have remained loyal to my profession. I may not excel at it but I'm good at many things. It is quite difficult and demanding to be a public figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm not limiting my questions, really, to just political life, sir. I did make a comment about that. But -- and I'm not in any way passing judgement or denigrating your various positions or your work at all. But you would agree with me, would you not, that in business or life or relationships or politics, one can at any given time have multiple different objectives, strategies, again to use the word "agendas" and sometimes those agendas can even conflict with each other. On the one hand you want to do A and at the same time you want to do B, which may conflict with each other but you try to reconcile, you try to balance them out as best you can; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to my political engagement, then it may be true. Sometimes you have to do things that you like doing; at other times, your party colleagues may ask you to do things that you do not particularly like. Sometimes you have to say things that you don't really mean. Life in the public light has to do with a great deal of compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- let me move on from that and come back to that in a few moments. But in terms of your involvement in getting humanitarian -- delivery of humanitarian aid and you've talked about that a bit in your direct examination. If I'm not wrong, you talked about taking some humanitarian aid to Tuzla; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, I took it there personally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the Tuta-Stela case, you were asked whether your attitude or the attitude of ODPR in Croatia changed depending on whether or not at any given time, for example, the Croats and Muslims were in conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, did that conflict cause you or your agency to change its practices or policies. You said at the time they did not, I'll just tell you that. You said at the time they did not change. Those circumstances did not change your attitude. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what it was that I said specifically in that case, but I know that the attitude did not change although I do not wish to conceal the fact that it was under psychological pressure. The individuals working in humanitarian organisations are only human beings. They work under pressure. They have their emotions, their perceptions and knowledge. It isn't that easy to witness a scene of massacred individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... in the Tuta-Stela case in which the witness testified, please give the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and I was about to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To be fair to you, witness, and let me just give you the fuller context and then I want to go on from that, building on that, if you will. Counsel, I'm referring to page 11029, starting at line 23. Just let me read this to you, Dr. Zoric, and counsel for Mr. Prlic has a copy of the same transcript and I'm sure that if I read something wrong, I will be corrected. You said during your testimony at that time, you said, "At times," I'm starting at line 23, "At times there were certain tensions which I tried to calm down and also if I may add, with regard to what the Prosecutor asked," in that case, "whether after the conflict in BH between the Muslims and Croats, there were some changes in our attitude to refugees. I must emphatically say no, that our attitude to them did not change." Then you go on in that passage to talk about, "I was the one who led," at the time you said, "several convoys to Tuzla," and then skipping a couple of lines, and counsel will see those, and you went on to say, "Had my attitude or anyone's attitude to those refugees changed, somebody in Sarajevo would have begrudged me that and very seriously." My question to you further on that, Doctor, is when you say that if your attitude or your practice had changed at that time, someone in Sarajevo would have begrudged you very seriously, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably I would not have been given the accreditation had I displayed discriminatory conduct toward the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the country itself. I was given accreditation to be ambassador there, I was well-received there and I am still travelling to that country frequently. I have many ties with that country and I feel quite at ease in Sarajevo, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
