utterances.text: If I understand what you've told us now is your political standing or your acceptance or the peoples' attitude toward you would have changed for the negative if you had changed your practices at the time, if you stopped giving aid because of that situation or said, "Well, now the Muslims and Croats are fighting each other, no more aid." You understood that that would have affected your standing at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe it's a mischaracterisation and if I may, and I believe the gentleman was talking about accreditation when he went to, as we all know, when you become an ambassador, I think that's what he meant, not about the -- if Mr. Scott could please rephrase the question and be accurate with the facts and maybe even ask a non-leading question but I don't think that's what the gentleman meant and I think it's a mischaracterisation of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me go back, sir, which is exactly the reason -- rather than characterise something is exactly the reason I simply quoted your previous sworn testimony in the Tuta-Stela case and you said and I'll read it again. "Had my attitude or anyone's attitude to those refugees changed, somebody in Sarajevo would have begrudged me that and very seriously." I will simply, in light of Mr. Karnavas's comment, I will just ask my previous question again. When you say that someone in Sarajevo would have begrudged you that very seriously, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question. Presumably you'd like to know whether I engaged in humanitarian activities in order to paint a better picture of my person in Sarajevo. I engaged in humanitarian work because that was my personal commitment and I did not get any pecuniary reward for that, it was merely something that I wanted to do as a human being. But if I found myself in a similar situation again where there were people who needed assistance that I could provide, I would engage in that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let me go to another topic and then I'll come back and see if we can tie the two together. We've heard extensive evidence in the courtroom and I don't think there's any dispute about it, in fact, that in Croatia during this period 1991, 1992, had gone through a terrible war. We know about the situation in Vukovar which was terrible. The case about that, in fact, was brought in this Tribunal. We know that at the time the JNA or the Serbs occupied approximately one-third of Croatia's territory. It was a difficult time in Croatia, correct, to say the least?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a difficult time and you described it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of the international political scene, Croatia was also concerned with the continuing integrity of its own borders and in fact reclaiming the territory that was then occupied by the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every country, including Croatia, wishes to preserve its national -- its territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And sir, would it be fair to say that just as you wanted to preserve your best standing, as I suppose we all do, you wanted to preserve your best standing in the political community in Sarajevo when you were ambassador, at the same time in these terrible and difficult circumstances, Croatia wanted to maintain its best standing in the international community; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not only out of the scope but now he's asking for some sort of an expert opinion. I don't know how the gentleman can now opine with respect to Croatia itself. You know, with the international community versus what? In what capacity? With respect to Bosnia? I mean, if he could lay some sort of a foundation but again I don't see the relevancy particularly the scope of my direct examination. So perhaps Mr. Scott can tell us a little bit. I don't wish to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you don't want to object, Mr. Karnavas, then don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can't help it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To respond to the foundation, Your Honour, that was exactly again which I was careful to go back and review so there would be no doubt of the foundation of this witness. Senior government official, vice-president of one house of parliament, ambassador, party leader, et cetera, et cetera. And if this man cannot voice any view on what was happening in Croatia at the time, then I'm not sure who else can except a handful of other people that would have held higher positions. I think it is directly relevant and I think if the Chamber will allow me another couple of questions, you will see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, this may be a very naive question, but do you question this because of the facts you're referring to or because of the credibility of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it relates to the substance of positions in this case going to the merits of the case. And I have -- I want to put questions to the witness about things directly related to matters in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which period, Your Honour? If it's 1999, I know we heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's -- okay. Well, I was under the impression that we're talking about 1999, I must confess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know why. I said that we're during the time when Croatia was occupied, at war, after Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned all of this -- okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will be happy to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I withdraw my objection. If it's 1992, 1993, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to make it clear to the witness that you're speaking about the 1992-1993 period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, and to be clear on that, I am referring to the 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, the time that you were in parliament and the preceding time and the very events and circumstances that I outlined to you a few moments ago about which I suspect there is no controversy in the courtroom, the circumstances facing Croatia during this period of time. Now, when I asked you about that, I don't know, we've lost the screen, the question that was last pending before the intervention. But my question to you was this: At that particular point in time, faced with those conditions, I think where we left off was the proposition that the State of Croatia, your government certainly wanted to maintain the best standing possible in the international community; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that every government except for the one who desires isolation wishes for that sort of support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it is a very political question that is put to you, since the Prosecutor is asking you what the position of the government was. I was under the impression that you were in the opposition. So little by little, I'm wondering, you were in the opposition so you were opposed to Tudjman, to the HDZ; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I took up the position, the high ranking position in the government was at the time of the coalition government. In 1991, a coalition government was set up, a government of national unity. There were no confrontations at the time because what was at stake was the very survival of the country. Subsequently, we were confronted -- we confronted one another on some issues and on others, we agreed. As far as I'm concerned, personally, I both agreed with them on some matters and disagreed on others. I was able to voice these agreements or disagreements through a given democratic procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Chamber might allow me and I apologise, Mr. President, I certainly don't want to cut across the President but if the Chamber might allow me, I intend to get to some of those questions but if I could finish this line of inquiry first, but I do very much intend to touch upon your questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question, following question from all that and I'm sorry that with all the number of interventions, perhaps the flow has been broken a bit, but my point to you, yes, you said a moment ago and I think we may have lost it again, of course every country wants to have - just leaving the screen now - the best standing possible. And my question to you on that is: We've heard an awful lot about Croatia's assistance to refugees and the sending of humanitarian aid into Bosnia-Herzegovina or the transit of humanitarian aid through Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina which is not disputed, by the way, is not disputed, but can you tell the Chamber, sir, based on all your political involvements and experience including as an ambassador to another state, what would have happened to Croatia's standing in the international community if they had just basically said, "No more humanitarian aid to Bosnia. We're cutting it all off. No more refugees. We will not send a single additional humanitarian convoy into Bosnia. Never again." What would Croatia's standing have been in the international community if they had taken that position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, is that not a question calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour, I think it's any political experienced politician, I think, and I think the Judges, you can probably draw your own conclusions, frankly. What do you think, what do you think the international community -- he's a political leader of that country, Your Honour. Who else can we expect -- who else do we ask that to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: He is asked to speculate what would happen if and that is speculation, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if that's the -- Your Honour's conception of speculation, I think I can ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you think would have happened, sir? What do you think if Croatia had taken that position, do you think Croatia's position would have remained the same, the high-standing -- a supported position in the west and in the UN and the international community? Or might that community have taken a very different view toward Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether I am entitled to complaining to the questions of the Prosecution in the cross-examination, because this is not my witness, but as a Defence counsel, and a party to the proceedings, I think I can say that if this is not speculation in the area of politics and if a person who albeit with political experience is supposed to say his opinion what would have happened if, for example, my grandfather had been Hungarian, whether I would be Hungarian. What is the point of all this? With all due respect, I don't see the point in all this. I wanted to say this much but I think this is wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, your question calls for speculation indeed, but your question is so obvious that the question is obvious as well -- the answer is obvious as well. So unless you have another follow-up question to tie, to make a link with another topic, I will allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Chamber's view is that that is -- the answer is so obvious to the extent that it would be essentially common knowledge then I'll ask the Chamber to take judicial notice of that fact that we can all understand based on our common experience that it probably have not have improved Croatia's standing in the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say that it is obvious, all you have to do is to look at Burmania [as interpreted][Realtime transcript read in error "Romania"] today whenever there is catastrophe, humanitarian catastrophe, you see that if international humanitarian organisations do not intervene then there is a problem. Now you're asking a question to the witness and he can only answer and give an obvious answer. It would be interesting to see what he will say but it's all relative. I didn't say Romania I said Burma.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just -- and I will move on and I would just again say for the purposes of the record that if someone that combines the various positions of this person can't express a view on that, I'm not sure who would be able to. He was a senior official in providing refugee and humanitarian aid. He was a senior party official. He was the vice-president of one house of parliament. He was an ambassador to another country. If he doesn't understand something about international politics and what taking that action would do to the standing of the Republic of Croatia in the international community, I'm not sure who else could express a view on that. It seems to me directly relevant to the case. Of course Croatia had powerful motivations not only -- perhaps many, undoubtedly many to do the right humanitarian thing, but there was also a political dimension to this as well and it's directly relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just very briefly. First, the question could have been asked in a leading fashion, perhaps it would not have drawn as many complaints, but more importantly, we've indicated and established that Croatia did sign on to certain international agreements, they have obligations, so obviously there might have been some repercussions but I don't think -- how is this related to the case? I fail to see unless Mr. Scott is going to show somehow that Croatia did not abide by its obligations under the circumstances. I think that's what's at issue. Perhaps if he could just move on but otherwise, it is speculative and I can just draw one example. What would happen if, say, one permanent member of the Security Council were to bomb one of the capitals in Europe? Well, they did, they bombed Belgrade and what happened? Nothing. So it is kind of speculative. Everybody complained but at the end of the day, the US did what it wanted to do. Same thing with Iraq, they invaded Iraq, they're occupying Iraq. So I think it is speculative but how does this advance the case? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think on that I will move on. I will move on. I hope the point's been made. As Mr. Karnavas has said many times in the last two years, I hope the Chamber gets the point. As to the examples Mr. Karnavas made, that further proves the Prosecution's point. I don't think the standing of the United States in the international community and in Europe is particularly higher after taking its positions and doing what it's done in Iraq; I think it's had a dramatically detrimental effect on the standing of the United States in the international community which proves my point. It is directly relevant, Your Honour, to the case and we will argue at the appropriate time but I'm not going -- we have to move on to other topics. If anyone expects me just because I am an American to defend some of the positions of my government, you are mistaken. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let's go on to another topic, sir. In terms of your humanitarian work, your refugee work, your work as an ambassador, is it correct that you have very good and fair relations with President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that I had good relations with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Judges, in fact, that sometime after the war that President Tudjman, in fact, awarded to President Izetbegovic and Haris Silajdzic Croatia's highest national decorations?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. President Tudjman decorated both President Izetbegovic and Mr. Silajdzic with the highest Croatian national decoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic arising out of your testimony in the Tuta-Stela case. You said there, and counsel, I'm referring to page 10981 starting at line 3. "People were in a way always going towards the centres of their own republics so it was quite logical for people from the Croatian areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina to study in Zagreb or Split and not in Sarajevo." Then going on down the page, you say, "The interest was in the life of their own people, nation, not of their own republic." What did you mean by that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was interpreting the sociological fact of the affiliation of individual peoples in ex-Yugoslavia. It is a fact that Croatia [as interpreted] was made up of federal units called republics but it's also a fact that it was inhabited by peoples, some that didn't all live in just one republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies for interrupting you, if you will allow me just to correct the record at page 56, line 2, I assume you meant to say it is a fact that Yugoslavia was made up of federal units, you said Croatia. I assume you meant Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were clear identities. With the arrival of democracy, these identities developed, but Yugoslavia had to be split into its republics, its federal units. As a consequence, tensions arose. As you know, initially, it was Croatia's position that Yugoslavia should be reorganized to become a confederation. Milosevic's position was that it should become a unitarian state. He also thought that in the case of his own people, the ethnic principle should be followed to the effect that all persons belonging to his people should live in one unit; but in the case of Kosovo, he advocated another principle, the historical principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translation, I'm sorry. I apologise for cutting across you but because of the time constraints that we all have to operate under, my question to you is not so much about Milosevic and the views of various politicians in Yugoslavia at the time, but more at the level of many of the people. Let me be very clear, I'm not saying all people. But your statement in the Tuta-Stela case that I read to you just a moment ago suggests that at least for many people, there was a stronger bond, there was a stronger affinity, a connection, to their people and their nation, and I'm using the two words that you used in your testimony, as opposed to the political entity that they found themselves in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was such groups and individuals, that is correct. It's a sociological fact. And that has been the case for many years and it reflected itself in the destinations of their migrations, where they sought a better life for them and their families. Some people thought that there was no future for them in the areas where they had come from so that they migrated toward their own republic so that many Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina went into the direction of Zagreb rather than Sarajevo. That is a well-known fact. I just wanted to say that the political developments were -- could even -- could accelerate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just building on that, if I could take you to another part of your previous testimony. Counsel, I am at page 10984 starting at line 2, you talk about there the identifying something a city or a town as a capital. And you said -- I'm not directly quoting you here because of the length of the passage but I'll quote you directly in a moment. The point you were making was to identify something as the "capital would mean ..." and now I am quoting you, "... something entirely different for a Serb or Croat not Sarajevo." "So when a Bosniak says Bosnia and Herzegovina, he or she, they do not mean the same thing that Croats do when they say Bosnia and Herzegovina." Can you tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed the misfortune of that country that not all people who lived there, who are citizens of that country, who are constitutive parts of that country do not see it in the same fashion. All of them speak about Bosnia-Herzegovina but when you ask them what that country is like or what it should be like, then you see that there are great differences among them and those differences, as you know, had even tragic conflicts as their consequence. I think that conflicts of the kind that took place in BiH unfortunately, but accurately show the amount of differences in that country, which is small, much too small for such huge differences. And at times, it couldn't manage those differences or at least not everybody could manage those differences and that is why such tragic events occurred. It is obvious that the country needed the assistance of both neighbouring countries and the international community as a whole. It is good that it received that assistance or aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to intervene to ask Mr. Scott the following. I am slightly astonished, as you know the cross-examination is not -- the scope of the cross-examination is not limited and the Trial Chamber has mentioned it on numerous occasions but the cross-examination should mainly stem from the questions put by the Defence and mainly it should deal with the refugees, humanitarian aid and humanitarian convoys, so on and so forth. But now, you are using the Tuta-Stela transcript, you are quoting what the witness said then. You could have brought this witness actually as a Prosecution witness and now we're talking about something quite different. Time is precious in this case and the topics that you are mentioning with this witness you could perhaps talk about these things with other witnesses and you are quite far from what this witness came to talk about. He came to testify on very precise questions and now you are talking about all sorts of topics. You were given four hours, that is true, but you are not rationally using the time. This, for me, I call this a waste of time. I don't know where you are going to. You are biding for time and you could just ask to have the transcript admitted into evidence, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We will be asking to have the transcript admitted into evidence in light of the questioning, Your Honour. We have absolutely no problem with his prior testimony coming in addition to his testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I could not have taken that -- I was not considering that scenario previously because that's the first of I've heard of that, so of course if Mr. Karnavas wants to do that that's up to him to file his motion. I do submit, number one, in terms of time, I'm -- and I don't want to waste the Chamber's time, but at the same time, I'm well within my time limits. I'm not even close, not even close to the four hours and I do think it's directly relevant. I think it relates to -- I think it relates to the positions and views of this witness, the Chamber should be informed of in assessing his evidence and the weight of his evidence. I think he has information that can assist the Chamber. The Chamber has, in the last two years, heard extensive evidence about the political views and even when sometimes people use the same words, they mean something entirely different. And I thought when I saw, when I reviewed this witness's testimony and what he said in the last two passages that I put to him including even when a Bosniak says the words Bosnia and Herzegovina and when a Croat says the words Bosnia and Herzegovina, it means two different things. It seems to me that that's something directly -- that's clearly relevant to this case. Beyond that, Your Honour, relating to the scope, I do believe -- number one, I do believe it's in the scope of cross-examination. That's my first position, number one. Number two, I would refer the Chamber to Rule 90 -- excuse me, 90(H)(i) which specifically states ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment please. I will read what we have stated in our decision on the 24th of April, 2008, on page 7, paragraph F. Rule 90(H)(i) of the rules. The cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the evidence in chief and the matters affecting the credibility of the witness and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examination party to the subject matter of that case. The Trial Chamber may request the party leading the cross-examination to explain how is the question put to a witness relevant. The Trial Chamber will not allow that the cross-examination go overboard and may reject all inappropriate questions and all questions that are not credible as well as all repetitive questions and irrelevant questions. This is what we've stated. This is our ruling. This is our decision. So you can raise various topics with this witness, but one must bear in mind that you can say the following: You said this in answer of a question put to you in examination in chief but I am putting this to you, and so on and so forth. You can also put questions relating to the credibility, et cetera, et cetera. So you have to frame yourself with respect to the examination in chief and not go overboard as I'm under the impression now. So please proceed. We will be more vigilant in controlling the proceedings and if we make rulings, we have to apply them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course and the passage that you just read a moment ago, it quotes from Rule 90(H)(i), and I refer the Chamber, as I was about to a few moments ago, to specifically that language which is found both in the rule and in the Chamber's guidelines which says, "... and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party," in this case, the Prosecution, "to the subject matter of that case." I am well within both the rule and the Chamber's guideline. Now whether it's irrelevant or not, is -- I believe that I've said why I think it is relevant so I'm within the scope of cross-examination, I'm well within my time limits and it is relevant. I agree, if I went on for hours and hours about something, I would agree. I've asked a couple of questions about this topic. I don't think it can be considered abusive. But in any event, I was finished with that topic. To return to the topic in fact that the President raised, I hope, Mr. President, since you raised the topic you will consider it to be within the scope and relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you were a, again, a member of the Social Liberal Party which was the largest opposition party to Croatia -- excuse me, in Croatia, my apologies, in Croatia during the 1993-1994 period and perhaps thereafter, you were also at that time as we've indicated the vice-president of the Chamber of Counties. Can you tell us who the head of the HSLS was at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was Mr. Drazen Budisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And within the Social Liberal Party at the time that you were a member of parliament, did it have something -- I don't know how it translates out in English but something called the reduced board?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What term -- perhaps there's a better term than reduced board, perhaps you can say it in your own language and the translators might be able to assist us. Or perhaps that's exactly what it's called.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called "malo vijece" in Croatian, which is approximately the small council or literally the small council and I was a member of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to characterise that some of us perhaps in other systems or countries might consider that like the executive board or the executive committee, the smaller, real senior managing group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at that time, apart from presumably the party president, Mr. Budisa and yourself, how many other people made up the reduced board of the HSLS?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were 10 to 15 of us, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention, please, to -- in the binder to Exhibit P 10420. P 10420, if you have that, please. I see that you have it. I can see that you have it. Sir, is it correct, and again building on some questions that the President began to put to you some minutes ago, as the opposition party, in fact, the HSLS was opposed to President Tudjman and the HDZ's policy toward Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, yes, not only regarding this issue. The opposition party has conflicting views on many issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we soon -- the -- we soon were in a position where there was disagreement about many issues and then the party was split into several smaller parties. At that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because time is precious as the President just reminded us. In the -- Exhibit P 10420 for the record is an article in The Independent, a British publication, dated the 30th of July, 1993. And in the second paragraph in the text, it says, "Croatia's President Franjo Tudjman is under increasing domestic pressure to end Zagreb's support for irredentist Croats in Herzegovina and to abandon his plans to share in a carve-up of Bosnia. However, Croatia's founding father is showing no signs of yielding to ever-louder demands for a policy reversal." Can you describe to the Judges, please, since you were very much in the political world at the time, the vice-president of one chamber of parliament, what was the domestic pressure referenced here concerning President Tudjman's policy towards Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the different parties, individuals, and groups voiced different opinions with regard to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were various proposals coming either from the local level or from the international community as to how the situation in the countries should be settled. Some of them supported the Vance-Owen Plan, others the Stoltenberg Plan, others were in favour of leaving it down to the local level to solve the situation. There was a flurry of activities at the international level, at the levels of the countries, locally, including Croatia. Everybody voiced their different opinions including the political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, and we know political disagreement is common to virtually every political system, I think, at least where dissent is allowed. But if I can ask you to skip a paragraph down to where it says, "On Wednesday, leaders of Croatia's 15 opposition parties united for the first time to oppose Mr. Tudjman's aim of Bosnian partition. 'Croatia's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina needs a turnabout,' Drazen Budisa," the leader of your party, "the main opposition Social Liberal Party told the daily Vecernji List. 'It is not too late to reach the agreement with Muslims,' he was quoted as saying." Now, in the view of your party, Mr. Budisa, yourself, you were a member of the governing board of that party, why did Croatia's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina need a "turnabout"?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there's a factual error there, an exaggeration. Croatia had never had 15 significant parties that would have had 15 leaders. We could have considered there to have been four or five significant political parties in Croatia at the time and today. Secondly, isn't it typical for a politician to speak of a turnabout. Barack Obama's main word is change and not support, he's calling for change. Leaders of the opposition always call for change. Therefore, the requests put forth by the opposition leaders are legitimate, they may be more or less acceptable, and it is the job of the head of state to move within certain set limits and as you know, the international community had a very active part to play in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we've heard a lot about that. But my question to you now is very specific and it isn't whether there were 13 opposition parties or 15. That's not my question. It says, "Croatia's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina needs a turnabout." Now, in order for there to be a turnabout, there has to be, first of all, a current policy, a present policy. What was Croatia's current policy as of 30 July 1993, and what it had been in the previous months, what was the policy which your party said had to be turned about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were able to see yesterday, in Croatia, the political leaders often times spoke of matters they didn't know enough about, of matters they didn't have firsthand knowledge of. The first delegation of that parliament, a member of which was Drazen Budisa responded to the invitation by Mr. Praljak who sits here and as you are well aware, that party had different opinions on many matters and I personally parted ways with Mr. Budisa because we disagreed. You have that individual still alive and well and you can ask him personally what it was that he meant by saying that. The fact of the matter is that he brooked a failure not success with such political speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The point, sir, is not whether Mr. Budisa's position then or now is successful. The question is the -- what was happening at this time. Now, you've told this Chamber in no uncertain terms that the HSLS was the largest opposition party. Mr. Budisa was the head of that party. You were a member of that party and vice-president of the Chamber of Counties and a member of the party's governing board. So when HSLS took this position against being critical of Tudjman's policy toward Bosnia-Herzegovina, I'm sure you knew exactly what the policy was that you were opposing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, it's the individual here that's taken -- that's expressing this position as the leader. Now, we don't know whether it's his personal or whether it's the party's, that's number one. Number two, as the witness indicated, the gentleman is alive and now, you know, and he could be called to explain what exactly that individual meant but to ask this witness to opine on what somebody else's thoughts are, I think, he's asking for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not asking for opinion, I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree with you, Mr. Karnavas. This witness was part of the executive committee of the party. We have a document of British origin that seems to indicate that there was a political change. Does the witness know? Does he not know? Mr. Witness, you did not answer the question put to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all of us in Croatia including the ruling party and the opposition parties wanted the conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina to be put to a stop and we wanted normalcy to be restored. The opposition parties including the one I was a member of was not always too happy with the manner in which there were attempts to achieve this or the speed at which this was done. I believe that this -- these were discussions on the eve of the reaching of the Washington Agreement which as you know was signed by representatives of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe that the agreement was a sort of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this was not on the eve of the Washington Agreement, the date of this article is the 30th of July, 1993. 30th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we can just move forward, then, because perhaps if I refer you to some other part of the article, you can assist us. If you will skip down several paragraphs, you will find a paragraph that starts with the words, "Former associates," and for those following in English, it is the third paragraph on the second page. It says, "Former associates say Mr. Tudjman is obsessed with the division of Bosnia and reluctant to abandon Herzegovina hardliners because their financial support helped propel him to power. He rejected the opposition's proposals. Those who proposed changes in policy seek to destabilize both Croatia and the ruling party, the steering committee of his Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) said." What was the reaction, sir, to your party of which you were a governing member to President Tudjman's and the HDZ's reaction essentially dismissing your opposition? What was your party's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every party including mine presented such positions as were felt were most favourable for the party at the time. The position of the official policy of Croatia in that regard, as I see it today, was to achieve the integration of the Republic of Croatia as soon as possible and with as few victims as possible. One of the aspects related to that was the stabilization of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, was this understood by all the different actors in the politics in Croatia alike, it's very difficult to say. The opinions professed differed. The only thing we can draw upon ultimately are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely the case. If I can direct your attention skipping one more paragraph to the last paragraph and -- excuse me, I have several questions for you about that. It says, "Critics fear that carving up Bosnia will set a precedent for the dismemberment of Croatia, which still has its own festering territorial dispute. Serbian rebels control a third of the republic's territory and want to join their Bosnian brethren in creating a Greater Serbia. There are also many Croats who believe Zagreb's continued support for Croatian extremists in Bosnia will result in international sanctions on Zagreb which would bury the Croatian economy." Now, can you assist the Chamber with this? Can you explain the point being made as to what was the basis of the concern that when it says, "There was a fear that carving up Bosnia would set a precedent for the dismemberment of Croatia by the Serbs." Can you explain that to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, at the time, one-third of Croatia was under occupation. As you know, the Serbs who were in control of the territory at the time were calling for an independent state of their own. Likewise, it was common knowledge that part of the international community back in 1994 offered the so-called Z-1 plan. Under the plan, a state within a state was to be formed in Croatia whereby the Serbs in Croatia would practically be given their own state with all the attributes and hallmarks entailed; their currency, government, police, army, borders. For Croatia, the only thing it envisaged was the obligation for Croatia to finance all of that, and it was supposed to be some sort of a federal Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I apologise but wasn't the fundamental problem was that in the view of many in Croatia at that time, including the opposition, the various opposition parties, the concern was that Croatia's policy toward Bosnia was in fundamental contradiction of its own territorial interest in terms of preserving its own territory and if -- to the extent that Tudjman supported a carve-up of Bosnia, that was inconsistent with refusing the Serbian carve-up of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know how President Tudjman could have attained his goal. A war is a big game where not everyone needs to win. Very often in 1992, 1993, 1994, the international community offered different agreements and settlements and the statesman ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question to you was very --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please. Please. Wasn't there -- wasn't the position of the critics, here referred to as critics and your party was one of those critics, the position was that there was a fundamental inconsistency with the HDZ policy to carve up one country, that is, Bosnia, while at the same time refusing the Serb's rights to carve up Croatia? If one country can carve up another country then everyone can do it; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Croatia wasn't carving up Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, was there a division within the country, yes, it was divided and there were different solutions for how to divide the country internally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't want to go through this entire article with you again. But back on the very first paragraph that I directed your attention to, the second paragraph in the article, "Croatia's president, Franjo Tudjman is under increasing domestic pressure to end Zagreb's support for irredentist Croats in Herzegovina and to abandon his plans to share in a carve-up of Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I remind everyone that this is an article written by a journalist. That's the journalist's position. That's the journalist's position. So that journalist can hold whatever position he wishes when he writes the article. Now when he goes to the quotes, there at least we know who said what but this is something that the journalist -- now if he wants to bring the journalist in to vouch for that but he's asking the witness to accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say a few words, only that in my view, of course what Mr. Karnavas said that it was a journalist's opinion. On the other hand, again in I believe in paragraph 4 which was already quoted, it says, and I quote, "On Wednesday, leaders of Croatia's 15," it may have been, I don't know, probably fewer, "opposition parties," because the doctor has already said that there is no 15 opposition parties, "united for the first time to oppose Mr. Tudjman's aim of Bosnian partition." And here is a quotation again, "Croatia's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina needs a turnabout." It is what was said by Budisa, by Mr. Drazen Budisa, that is the leader at that time, of the main opposition Social Liberal Party to the daily Vecernji List. Now, if Dr. Zoric doesn't want to reply to the Prosecution's question concerning the paragraph which was later on quoted and asked about then I would like to ask Dr. Zoric if what he and the time his party meant and I quote again, "to oppose Mr. Tudjman's aim of Bosnian partition," and Mr. Budisa said "Croatia's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina needs a turnabout." So what, in his view, that turnabout meant and how the turnabout could have been implemented? It is my question, Dr. Zoric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, I do support this question asked by Judge Prandler. I wanted to ask the same question. This is at the very heart of the matter when we look at this article, of course it is drafted by a journalist but it seems to make references to political leaders, local political leaders who made specific statements. So please answer Judge Prandler's questions because it is a very relevant one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is what happened at the time, the proposals coming from Zagreb and from this group of people in particular were to the effect that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina had to establish cooperation with the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that there was a need to engage in the discussions about how this country would be structured and that these discussions should be different from the discussions that were being conducted at the time. The opposition opposed vehemently the plans put forth by the international community. They repeatedly said that for instance the Vance-Owen Plan was very dangerous for the future of the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are a diplomat and you answer in a diplomatic manner. This text relates to problems of inner policy, so put aside the international dimension of it. When you read this article, let me convey to you my impression. One is under the impression that there was a specific political attitude or line defended by many opposition parties in Croatia and according to this article, there was an objective, Tudjman's objective which is to partition Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, if we go by this article, there are disagreements in this political line and some political parties, including yours, apparently, seem to say that there is a risk, a danger to go, if we go along the lines of partition, because there could be a sort of boomerang effect on Croatia itself, a third of which is occupied by Serbs. It is therefore necessary, they say, to change lines, to change policies, to have a turnabout which could account for the political division within this agreement between the political parties. This is what the article says. Do you agree with the fact that partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been envisioned; yes or no? Is it because there were Serbs on a third of your territory that some, like you said, "Do not go down that line because it is a dangerous way." With regard to the Croats in BiH, we need to develop another approach. Is this a way in which you can interpret this article? Does this article mirror the inner political debates you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You have interpreted the article correctly. The only thing that I cannot confirm is that the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina was envisaged or rather, that there was a partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina envisaged officially or that any of the individuals professed that officially. The only thing I can admit is that there were many plans around and as for the opinions of particular individuals, I don't think we should waste any time on them if there were any such individuals. What we have here, after all, is only a newspaper article, in my view. With all due respect, I heard Mr. Prosecutor say that he's not too happy about what his country is doing in Iraq. At the same time, I'm sure that I can find many newspaper articles coming from either his country or other countries who speak favorably of the president of his country just as there are many articles who speak positively of the future leaders of that country and who advocate a positive change of policy in the US of A. What we are having is a discussion on political commitments or views. What I can confirm is that there were never any discussions or activities aimed at partitioning that country and in our view, and this is my view today as well, the plans put forth by the international community were deemed to be dangerous for the future of Croatia at the time. In my view, that country over there is still divided and it is divided in such a way that does not make matters look up for the future of that country. That sort of division cannot be beneficial for any country including Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, perhaps, last question before the break, come back to the intervention of Mr. Karnavas which I think was fully justified and what I was missing was a kind of a foundation-laying question. These passages, in particular the one referring to Tudjman being obsessed with the division of Bosnia. Would you agree that this was a correct description at that time of the political situation in Croatia or is the journalist wrong? Ms. Alaburic, it is a slightly directive question, quite a leading question but it leaves open the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say something to avoid misunderstanding. This may be a linguistic problem as well as a problem of fact that certain notions are perceived differently. Let us first say what we mean by saying the partitioning of Bosnia. We do not know what the journalist who is the author of this article meant, but I can tell you that we in Croatia implied different meanings at different times of this notion. At one point, we conceived of it as a division of Bosnia within a country that would have been a single country, therefore, a division into several entities so it would not have been a division of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At other times, what was meant was the division of the state of Bosnia in -- and thereby the disappearance of Bosnia as an internationally-recognised state. So let us first define what we are talking about before we proceed in our discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not much convinced by that because this speaks of Herzegovina hardliners. Herzegovina hardliners. So I think it's really clear. But I would like the witness to answer the question because it's really a founding question. Maybe the witness will tell this is all rubbish and nothing is true, this is an invention and I would like you, Dr. Zoric, to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will gladly answer your question. President Tudjman was not obsessed with the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the sense of breaking it up or annexing a part to Croatia. He knew he very well what international relations were like. He knew the balance of forces on the ground and he had a crystal clear objective he wanted to reach. That objective is a free Republic of Croatia, free on its entire territory. To achieve that objective, he had to be patient. He had to resist with weapons to provide armed resistance and he also had to attack. He also had to talk and as you know, he was able to achieve his goal. There are many documents, agreements signed by Dr. Tudjman. He signed them with President Izetbegovic and those documents always mention Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were conducive to bringing about peace in that country. In some of these agreements between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, mention is made of various proposals for the internal structure or territorial organisation of that country, the remit of the individual parts, et cetera. President Tudjman certainly wanted to preserve the status of constituent people to the Croats there, they had it in the former Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, though, I doubt that this is still the case today. And concerning all these questions that worried the public, I can only repeat that Croatia under the leadership of President Tudjman called upon the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you know, to vote at the referendum for the independence of that country which independence was advocated by the Bosnian Muslims too. If it hadn't been for that referendum, the independence would have been doubtful from a legal point of view. Croatia, while Mr. Tudjman was president, was amongst the first to recognise the independence of that country and Croatia was the first to send an ambassador there. I believe that these are clear enough indications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, what's your problem? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I ask Judge Antonetti as the President of the council to allow me the following question: Did the opposition, when they say the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mean its break-up under the Vance-Owen Plan or the status of constitutive people for Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this question could be put as part of the redirect but anyway, I shall take it up myself. Witness, you've heard what Mr. Praljak has just said. Can you answer his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that both options are possible. The opposition, in part, was against the Vance-Owen Plan which could have been an introduction to a negative outcome in Croatia, and as we're discussing newspaper articles, I would like to remind one in which a leader mentioned here spoke or rather said that he can imagine a federal Croatia. And after that, after a certain time, the Z-4 proposal was made. Some other leaders also joined in with such -- joined in with their respective statements. They were also against the Vance-Owen Plan, against any break-up and for unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina. In my opinion, President Tudjman always insisted on the preservation of the status of constitutive people for the Croats in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, this is not the solution that prevails today. The first question is whether the Croats are a constitutive people at all. And the other question is whether an ethnic Croat who lives in Mostar has the same right as an ethnic Croat who lives in Banja Luka. The fact is that they don't have the same rights and in my opinion, they should have. This also means that every Serb in Bosnia-Herzegovina should also have the same rights, whether he or she lives in Doboj or in Capljina and every Bosnian Muslims should have the same rights wherever he or she may live. The current situation is such that the people who live there are the ones who are least satisfied with it. People who live in Bosnia-Herzegovina know that this country is very difficult to run the way it is organised now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 12.30, we're going to break for 20 minutes. I'm looking at the clock. We're going to resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, would you be able to tell us how much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, under the circumstances, it's extremely difficult to predict because of all the interventions. So far, I've used just barely over half of my total time. I was given four hours. The Defence so far in total including all the follow-up examinations has been four hours and 46 minutes. The Prosecution so far has had two hours and 20 minutes so we've had only half as much time as the Defence. It's hard to say. If there was absolutely no interventions, if the witness gave short responsive answers we might finish by 1.45 but it's very doubtful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, in light of the discussions so far, the testimony so far concerning the article, P 10420, and the answers you've given, I have to put to you that the position that you're -- in large measure, in large measure, the position that you've state to the Court today is quite different than the position that you and your party took in 1993 and 1994. And the position you're stating today is a change of heart, perhaps, or a different position than the one you held at the time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The circumstances have also changed and the facts are different so that now, I hold a different position with regard to some issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, precisely. But, you see, Dr. Zoric, you can tell us that and it's fine for you to say, I've changed my mind, but what the Judges need to know and in response to the questions about the exhibit I put in front of you, my questions were not what you believe now, but what you and your party believed at that time in July 1993 and indeed in the months preceding July 1993. So to the extent as you've just indicated, you've given different answers, you've changed your view, then you haven't told us even yet and we don't have probably time, you haven't told us yet what your position was at that time. Now, in that regard, sir, I think the Chamber should know is it correct that in June 1995, you left the HSLS and joined Tudjman's party, the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But that wasn't in June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When was it, please?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, in September or October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: September or October 1995, you left the HSLS and joined Franjo Tudjman's party, the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we can go on to Exhibit P 10422. This is an article from Globus, a well-known Croatian publication. On the 28th of January, 1994, concerning an interview with the same Drazen Budisa who was your party head and in that sense superior at the time. Again, because of shortness of time, we don't have time to go through the entire article. But if you can please go well into the interview, sir, and for those following in English, to -- toward the top of the third page. If you can find, Dr. Zoric, if you can find please the passage, the paragraph that's starts, that's attributed to Mr. Budisa, it starts with the words, "Because President Tudjman is captured ..." and I want to give you a fair opportunity to find that so please tell me when you've found it. Do you have it yet, please?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It says there, and I won't read the entire paragraph but, "Because President Tudjman is captured by the concept of rearranging the former old Yugoslavia in completely different historical circumstances, he has pointed out several times that there is no solution to the Croat issue without an arrangement with Belgrade, and that our interest is the encompassing of the Croat ethnic territories. This is in itself neither correct nor wrong outside the historical context. Macek, the Croatian signatory of the 1939 agreement founding the Banat of Croatia also acted upon these bases." Sir, building on the testimony that or the topics and the information we've covered so far today, isn't this a further confirmation that what your party was opposed to in terms of Tudjman's policies towards Bosnia in 1993-1994, what your party was opposed to was his desires to establish the Croatian Banovina borders inside Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the assertions of one person from the leadership of the party. Even though that person is president, I did not agree with such positions so that a year later we parted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A year later you parted, but that was indeed Doctor -- or excuse me, Mr. Budisa's position as stated here; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but in politics, some things mature, they take their time. The reasons are not simple. Such statements contributed to my dissatisfaction and not only did I part with him, other people did too. I have already mentioned the party split into three parties due to a disagreement over crucial issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, let me ask you this: There was also -- already a reference to Mr. Macek, the Croatian signatory of the 1939 agreement that established the Banovina. In the next paragraph, there's a reference to a Dragisa, forgive me pronunciations if it's wrong, Cvetkovic --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- and can you tell us or remind the Judges, please, who was Dragisa Cvetkovic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because I have a university degree in history, otherwise I wouldn't be qualified to explain that here. Dragisa Cvetkovic was the prime minister of the kingdom of Yugoslavia and Vladko Macek was the president of the Croatian Peasant Party which at the time was the leading Croatian political party that enjoyed the support of the largest number of Croats not only in Croatia but also in Bosnia-Herzegovina and it's a political paradox mentioned in literature that even in some municipalities in Serbia, Macek had voters, people who voted for him. It is generally known that Cvetkovic and Macek signed an agreement about the restructuring of the kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1939. They thought that agreement would be the solution of the so-called Croatian national question in Yugoslavia. The subsequent development of the situation showed that -- or rather proved them wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the interviewer's question following the part that I read to you a moment ago, it says, "Do you think that Tudjman is trying to find his Dragisa Cvetkovic (prime minister of Yugoslavia, co-signatory of the 1939 agreement mentioned above) in Milosevic?" In other words, Tudjman wants to play the role of Macek and casting Milosevic in the role as Cvetkovic? Correct? That's the question by the interviewer.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it would be much more practical for this Court to invite the man who said what is -- what we can read here. I am not qualified to interpret his words. I am here to testify about refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the assistance we provided to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's not entirely correct, sir, as the Judges explained the rules and the scope of the examination. Sir, let me direct your attention another couple of paragraphs down in the next -- skipping over where Budisa says, "Today ..." Skipping over the next question and then when Budisa starts talking again, down in that paragraph, he says and I put this to you in -- particularly in light of the ongoing questions from this morning, "If the Croatian politics continues to aspire," I emphasise continues to aspire, "towards Herceg-Bosna being annexed to Croatia, then the question arises how we will retrieve our occupied areas. There is constant talk that the two-thirds of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina who will be left outside the Croat republic of Herceg-Bosna will be equal in all respects." Now, again, that was the issue over which Budisa and your party was taking issue with the HDZ and President Tudjman; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were in disagreement. We failed to understand how that could be prevented from reflecting upon Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next take you, please, then to Exhibit P 10409.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that there was a correction, there was a translation correction and there is a new copy of that document that's loose so hopefully everyone has it in front of them. If you don't then we will certainly assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've made several references in the last few minutes or some time that, you know, you would like to be confronted with your own words, perhaps, and so I'm doing that. This is an interview that you gave on the 13th of March, 1994 to Vijesnik; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can we all go forward with the understanding that you agree and confirm that you did give an interview to Vijesnik around this time, the 13th of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave many interviews at the time, among others, to Vijesnik. When exactly it would be hard for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, your position seems to be, and I've read this interview several times, your position in this interview appears to be that the Washington Agreement and this is now the interview is the 13th of March 1994, your position seems to be at the time that the Washington Agreement should be supported; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that that agreement could put an end to the conflict and make the warring parties sit at a table together. In my opinion, it's better to talk than to wage war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And once again, sir, can you agree with me that the Washington Agreement represented a fundamental shift of what had been President Tudjman's policy up until that time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a shift in his policy, but it's a fact that after talks and several attempts, an agreement was brought about, but it takes two to have an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the first paragraph after the box text, if you will, the first paragraph reading down through it, I'm going to touch on various parts of these in turn, but you say, "'The Croatian-Muslim agreement in Washington should be supported, but without any euphoria,' claims Damir Zoric, the vice-president of the Chamber of Counties and member of the reduced board of the HSLS. Zoric says that, 'This is maybe really about a strategic turn in Croatian policy.'" So this was a fundamental -- well, I'll use your word, it was a strategic turn from the previous existing Tudjman policy, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do consider that a shift, but a shift is not the same thing as is a turn. A shift means moving from one situation to another and then continue forward. But a turn is something else. It can mean abandoning one position and embracing another instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the time, you and your party viewed this or at least can I put it to you this way: Did you hope, did you hope at the time that this represented Tudjman abandoning the policy of partitioning Bosnia and establishing the Banovina borders?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, he needs to establish that fact. I want him to finish his cross but now this is a fact that's not been established. He needs to establish that that was Tudjman's policy as he understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the entire Prosecution case has presented that proposition and I've shown you two articles, the two articles that have just said clearly make that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The two articles are discussing somebody else's words. The gentleman is alive. He was here. He could have been brought during the Prosecution's case. Now, he needs to lay a predicate. That's his theory. Fine. He can state it as a theory but not as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't draft these documents, Mr. Karnavas. They say what they say and the presidential transcripts say what they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way and I know that the Defence doesn't like this evidence, but when you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to that as well. Why don't we tell the witness what the previous witness said on direct examination. Mr. Zuzul said quite clearly that that wasn't President Tudjman's policy. Why don't we say that and then ask him, now, do you disagree with Mr. Zuzul?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I assume that if the witness read --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not whether I like it or not. It's proper etiquette in court, lay a foundation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I assume that if Dr. Zoric read in the Croatian media about Mr. Zuzul's testimony he's already heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now we're saying that all our witnesses are confabulating. Quite interesting, the Prosecution witnesses come in and tell the truth; the Defence witnesses are confabulating. Sir, set the predicate. Ask the foundational questions and then there won't be any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We spent the last two years establishing the predicate, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir, let me ask you this to use your own words. Let me ask you this. Let me find if for you. On page 3 of the English translation and I'll have to help you find it, sir. You were asked at one point, if you can find this question, it's under the heading "The fatal Tito's youth." It says, "Does it mean that the HSLS will now be less critical towards the authorities? No, it does not. We did not criticise the HDZ only because of their catastrophic policy towards BiH and inside BiH." So perhaps you can tell us, sir, those are your words, what was catastrophic about Croatia's then existing policy towards BiH and inside BiH?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that question regardless of what the procedure dictates, I wanted to answer your previous question although it was qualified as a speculation, there is no reason why I shouldn't answer it. We were active in the public domain and spoke publicly on various issues mainly through TV broadcasts or newspaper reports. The political infrastructure or rather the infrastructure of the political parties at the time was insufficiently developed in order to enable us to speak specifically on all matters; however, it was part of the political competition where parties wanted to use up as much room as they could and be able to speak. Now, when it comes to this statement of mine you referred to, I believed at the time and I still believe that the Washington Agreement constituted a significant step forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I'm sorry that I started to interrupt you. Let me go back to what you said and what you were saying in answer to -- you said my previous question. Sir, you say you're relying on broadcasts, what you read the newspapers, et cetera. Sir, you were and I'm using the word government not in the sense of the executive branch, I'm talking about the government of Croatia as a whole, you were a senior member of that government, a senior member. Vice-president of one of the houses of parliament in the governing board of the largest top opposition party. Now, please, don't tell the Judges that you didn't understand what the politics in Croatia were at the time. You knew what Tudjman's policy was and you knew that you and your party presumably after the reduced board had decided its platform and its policy position, you knew that you, Mr. Budisa and the party opposed Tudjman's policy to partition Bosnia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I knew. How else would it have been an opposition party had it not been opposed to matters. Opposition parties normally do that. I have tried to answer your question but you keep interrupting me. I can answer every question you put to me even the one that I referred to a moment ago that remained unanswered by me before the break because of procedural issues. There isn't a single reason why I shouldn't answer every one of your questions. I can answer this one as well but please do not interrupt me. I wish to explain to you what my position is and what my answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber knows that the time constraints but assuming we won't finish today in any event, I'll let you go ahead. Say whatever you want to say.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do wish us to conclude today because I am a businessman. I have business to attend to. In answer to your question, yes, as an opposition party, we criticised the ruling party in all manners possible. We criticised, and I mean both the leader of the party and the members of the party. Oftentimes when opposition parties criticise the ruling party, this is done in a general way by way of specific illustrations, specific examples. Sometimes we disagree on policy decisions, on legislative decisions. Sometimes we are opposed to those, and I'm referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina now who are opposed to talks, who are opposed to the -- to those who propose certain solutions and I believe this was the case in this case at point. Very often, the political discourse includes platitudes and as I'm able to glean from this, I was the one using them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you, sir, to go to the part of your interview where you are asked -- and in English it's toward the top of the second page, if you can find the question, sir, please, "What do you think about the confederation of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina?" You say, "Croatia and BiH may begin certain inter-state relationships only after they have become sovereign in the whole areas they respectively occupy. Croatian interest is that BiH remains one unique country and that Croats in it be equal with other citizens." Now, when you say that these things can only be further addressed, "only after they have become sovereign in the whole areas that they respectively occupy," is it correct that you were talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina in it's entire internationally-recognised borders, not only that those borders would be respected but that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be, your word, "sovereign in that entire area"?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are my words and I stand by them today. I have always stood by them and will. Bosnia-Herzegovina ought to be sovereign in every inch of its territory as is the case with Croatia and with any other internationally-recognised country for that matter. Now, once these countries have resolved their fundamental issues and problems, will they engage into discussions about their mutual relations, cooperation, and accession to a higher level association, I believe this is something that can only be wished for at the international level. However, in order to accede to such associations, every country concerned must be -- must have sovereignty over its territory to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You go on, if I can direct your attention to page 4 in the English translation and if you can find, sir, the question that's put to you, "Can the implementation of the Washington Agreement encounter a serious resistance in a part of the ruling party or the opposition?" And you say there, I'm skipping the first paragraph although everyone in the courtroom has it, I'm not misleading anyone, "However, the implementation of the new policy could be very painful in Herzegovina. The policy of the Croatian-Muslim understanding is in the collision with the facts and emotions that presently exist. Therefore, one should be careful that the implementation does not collide with the reality. It is also the question whether the same people can implement two concepts that are so different and that went from war to alliance." If I could combine that, please, and ask you to hopefully save a few minutes, we might be able to finish today, at least my part, I can't speak for anyone else. Toward the bottom -- well, in the English towards the bottom of that page but after the question where it says, "Do you mean Mate Boban?" Then in the third paragraph in your answer, sir, you say, "Nowadays, their political leaders report that there are allegedly no problems in Herzegovina. However, it is very much so that there are problems in Herzegovina. People are confused because they waged the war for something, they lost their lives, children, husbands, property. More victims fell in the war against the Muslims than against the Serbs. Many ask themselves today: Why?" In both of those two passages that I just put to you, Dr. Zoric, isn't what you're saying here: This, again, Washington represented a fundamental shift. The people had thought that they were fighting, or at least many people, certainly not everyone, many people including the Herceg-Bosna leadership thought they were fighting for a part of Herceg-Bosna that would join and be part of Croatia and now, now as Washington finally evolved, this was an abrupt change of course which it was going to be difficult for people to accept? That's what you are expressing your concern about; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not a correct interpretation. I didn't say that the people fought and died for something that was to become a part of Croatia. There may have been individuals who did, but I believe that the -- that the majority of people who took part in that struggle did not find the sense in it because they thought that they were creating a better Croatia but because that they thought that they were creating this third entity, the Croat entity of the state of Bosnia.
